intro: Every day you describe people and things: a new teacher, your little brother, a pair of lost headphones, how you feel before a game. In Spanish, describing starts with two verbs that both mean to be, ser and estar, and with adjectives that change their endings to match what they describe.

This unit shows you how to choose between ser and estar: ser for who someone is, where they are from, what they are like, the time and events; estar for where someone is and how they feel or are doing right now. Then you will learn to make adjectives agree in gender and number, place them in a sentence, and compare people with más… que, menos… que, mejor, peor, mayor and menor.

By the end you will be able to describe a family member, a friend or a famous person in a clear paragraph, explain every verb you chose, and fix the most common mistakes English speakers make, like la casa blanco or la fiesta está en mi casa.
bigQuestion: How do Spanish speakers describe who someone is, how they are right now, and how they compare to others?

words.d: to be — identity, origin, traits, time, dates and events: soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son
to be — location, feelings and conditions: estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están
to be from, or to be made of — Soy de Chicago; La mesa es de madera
Where is it? — location always uses estar
happy, pleased — a feeling, so it uses estar: Estoy contenta
with ser: clever; with estar: ready
with ser: boring; with estar: bored
adjective — a describing word that matches its noun in gender and number
intelligent — one form for both genders; plural inteligentes
more… than — Ana es más alta que Luis
older — Mi hermana es mayor que yo; menor means younger

test.q: Which form completes the sentence? Yo ___ de Honduras.
test.why: Origin uses ser, and yo takes soy.

test.q: Which sentence says We are at the museum?
test.why: Location of people uses estar; nosotros takes estamos.

test.q: Which sentence says It's two o'clock?
test.why: Time uses ser; two o'clock is plural: son las dos.

test.q: What does Mi primo está aburrido mean?
test.why: Estar aburrido describes a feeling: bored.

choices: La fiesta está en el parque.
La fiesta es en el parque.
La fiesta estás en el parque.
La fiesta son en el parque.

test.q: Which sentence says My mom is a doctor?
test.why: Jobs use ser without un or una, and doctora matches mamá.

test.q: Choose the adjective: Las ventanas están ___.
test.why: Ventanas is feminine plural, so abiertas.
Ojos is masculine plural; café adds -s: cafés.

test.q: Which phrase says a great idea?
test.why: Grande becomes gran before a singular noun and means great; idea is feminine: una.

test.q: Which sentence says Luis is less tall than Ana?
choices: Luis es menos alta que Ana.
Luis es menos alto de Ana.
Luis es menos alto que Ana.
Luis está menos alto que Ana.
test.why: Menos + adjective + que; alto agrees with Luis.

choices: Mis abuelos son más mayores que mis padres.
Mis abuelos son mayor que mis padres.
Mis abuelos están mayores que mis padres.
Mis abuelos son mayores que mis padres.
test.why: Mayor needs no más and becomes mayores in the plural.

test.q: Which question asks what someone is like?
test.why: ¿Cómo eres? uses ser and asks about traits.

test.q: Choose the adjective: Mi hermana es muy ___.
test.why: Paciente ends in -e, so it has one form for both genders; hermana is singular.

test.q: What does La sopa está rica mean?
choices: The soup is rich in money.
The soup is from a rich family.
test.why: Estar rico describes how food tastes.

test.q: Which pair fits? Mi amigo ___ simpático, pero hoy ___ triste.
test.why: A personality trait takes ser; a feeling today takes estar.

write.prompt: Escribe un párrafo sobre una persona importante en tu vida. Write a paragraph in Spanish (6–8 sentences) that says who the person is and where they are from, describes their looks and personality, tells how they are or where they are today, and includes one comparison with más… que, menos… que, mayor or menor.
tips: Use ser for identity, origin and traits; use estar for location and how the person feels today.
Check every adjective against its noun: -o or -a, singular or plural.
Put most adjectives after the noun, and use tener for hair and eyes.
Use que in comparisons, and never write más mejor.
Read it aloud, then read again looking only at endings and accents.
